set.descent_text: The gully ends high on the face between the two peaks. From the top, one option is to descend south and traverse around toward Broken Hand Pass, which is slower going than it looks. The other is to continue along the Needle to Peak traverse and go up to either summit. Topping out on Crestone Peak and then descending into the South Colony Lakes valley brings you back past the base of the route.
set.approach: Reaching the east side of the Crestones starts at the lower South Colony Lakes parking area, which sits well below the old trailhead. A 4x4 helps on the road to it. From there a jeep road leads up past the original trailhead and on to the lakes. The route follows a gully on the wide northern wall that links the Needle and the Peak. Look for a shallow, left-leaning corner system roughly two thirds of the way from the Ellingwood Ledges line on the Needle toward the North Pillar of the Peak. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page gives the line and the top-out options; area page gives the trailhead and road. Single source per fact, so medium.

set.descent_text: Parties descend by rappelling the flow from V-threads in the ice, with a piton anchor in a sheltered alcove partway up the second pitch also in use. Once down at the steep snow ramp above the first pitch, stroll down and around the gentle snowfield back to the foot of the climb. A walk-off is also possible from the top: leave the notch and go left over the diamond-shaped wall, which is snowy third-class ground that is best done with plenty of daylight or route-finding experience. The slope above funnels avalanches and rockfall onto the climb, so do not linger at the belays.
set.approach: The flow lies on the north face of Crestone Peak, at the head of the Spanish Creek drainage. The usual way in follows that drainage, which is steep, brushy and slow, and in a dry early winter it can be mostly free of snow. A second way in starts at the South Colony Lakes trailhead and crosses the Bear's Playground by the third-class ridge of Humboldt Peak or through the low cirque beneath the Peak's northeast side, arriving above the diamond-shaped wall at the top of the route. The ice starts as a low notch at the foot of the Northwest Couloir and grows down toward the snowfield below. The face is exposed to avalanches and rockfall from the cliffs above. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page gives approach alternatives, rappel descent and walk-off. Rappel counts left out (one source).

set.descent_text: The route finishes on the summit of Crestone Needle. Descend by the standard route on the Needle, or follow the traverse over to Crestone Peak and come down the Red Gully. The south-facing gully directly below the summit is not a reliable way down; it ends in a cliff band.
set.approach: Approach from the Cottonwood Creek trailhead near the town of Crestone on the west, or from the South Colony Lakes trailhead on the east, to Cottonwood Lake. From the lake, scan the Needle's south side for a conspicuous maroon dihedral that leans right and rises out of the talus. Overhangs cap both walls of the dihedral, but a line of ice slips between them to a choke below a moderate snow slope. Do not follow the obvious snow line that ends at a gap in the ridge to the summit's west; the route escapes into the next gully to the right through a weakness in the right wall of the first gully. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page only: approach lake, key features and descent options.

set.descent_text: Rappel the route, which works but is not ideal, or walk off to either side while watching for avalanche danger. The walk-off to the south, on the right, leads toward the Masters Wall for more climbing.
set.approach: The falls sit just above the Cunningham Gulch road, on the left as you drive in, a short way past the signed forks, keeping right. The road is usually snowed in by midwinter, though ice often forms before that. The first short steep pitch starts a few minutes from the road. The creek above can be bypassed by an old roadcut or by hiking the hillside north of the creek. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page for the line, access and descent; area page for the seasonal road.

set.descent_text: Parties commonly set up a top rope from ice screws and then use a zero thread anchor in the ice to rappel.
set.approach: Drive or walk to the head of Cunningham Gulch. The flow is a broad, usually thick fall on the left side as you travel up the valley. Follow the approach used for the Master's Wall rock area, then continue farther up and to the left to the ice. It tends to form early, so it is a low-snow-year option. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Single route page; non-numeric facts only.

set.approach: Drive to the end of Cunningham Gulch. The gully is obvious on the right side as you go up the valley, and its first pitch is directly across the valley from Master's Wall Falls. It is a long, steady gully climb that suits early winter with little snow. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Single route page; no descent stated for the top.

set.approach: Start at the Wild Basin trailhead and follow the Thunder Lake trail past Ouzel Falls, which is a long winter approach once the road closes with snow. Leave the trail at about the point where North St. Vrain Creek can be followed upstream to the tributary that drains Eagle Lake. Go up that tributary past Mertensia Falls and through a forested headwall; a second headwall near treeline leads to the lake. Avalanche terrain is limited until you leave the St. Vrain valley, and from there on the snow needs careful assessment. These small flows are scattered west and southwest of the lake, beneath the upper ice and under Eagle's Beak, and they sit in avalanche terrain. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area page for approach; route page for the flows.

set.descent_text: Walk off by descending steep snow to climber's right.
set.approach: Start at the Wild Basin trailhead and follow the Thunder Lake trail past Ouzel Falls, which is a long winter approach once the road closes with snow. Leave the trail at about the point where North St. Vrain Creek can be followed upstream to the tributary that drains Eagle Lake. Go up that tributary past Mertensia Falls and through a forested headwall; a second headwall near treeline leads to the lake. Avalanche terrain is limited until you leave the St. Vrain valley, and from there on the snow needs careful assessment. The flow forms on broken cliffs north of the lake, a couple of hundred feet above it. Reaching it means climbing a wide snow slope of moderate angle, and a boulder at the base makes a handy belay spot. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area and route pages.

set.approach: Start at the Wild Basin trailhead and follow the Thunder Lake trail past Ouzel Falls, which is a long winter approach once the road closes with snow. Leave the trail at about the point where North St. Vrain Creek can be followed upstream to the tributary that drains Eagle Lake. Go up that tributary past Mertensia Falls and through a forested headwall; a second headwall near treeline leads to the lake. Avalanche terrain is limited until you leave the St. Vrain valley, and from there on the snow needs careful assessment. The upper ice lies southwest of the lake and high above it. The snow slopes between the lake and the base are prime avalanche terrain. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area and route pages; no descent stated.

set.descent_text: Parties on this buttress commonly walk down the Hallett Couloir or down couloirs into Chaos Canyon. When avalanche risk is high, the alternative is going down the line you climbed by rappel, using trees and boulders as anchors.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. The route is on the cliffs above the lake, in the scree-filled gully between Butterfingers and Left of the Cleft. Climb the gully to a tower with a prominent dihedral. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area page gives approach and shared descents; route page gives its location.

set.descent_text: Parties on this buttress commonly walk down the Hallett Couloir or down couloirs into Chaos Canyon. When avalanche risk is high, the alternative is going down the line you climbed by rappel, using trees and boulders as anchors.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. The line follows the central couloir, the prominent gash that splits the East Buttress. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area and route pages.

set.descent_text: Once past the first section, a rappel off a nearby tree reaches the ground. From the top, walk off leftward along the ridge to a saddle, then curl back beneath the cliff to the base. That walk-off is only advisable when the snow is stable.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. It sits at the left end of the Tastee Freeze buttress, in a conspicuous chimney that cuts two small roofs, lower than Tastee Freeze itself. Reach that buttress as for Tastee Freeze: from the end of the trail at Emerald Lake, scramble directly uphill to a little notch above the talus. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page gives its own walk-off and rappel option.

set.descent_text: From the top of the buttress, head down the ridge toward the Dream Lake chutes and follow them down to Dream Lake. Rappelling the route of ascent is a fallback when avalanche risk is high.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. Begin a short way to the right of Tastee Freeze, beneath a clear dihedral that faces left. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page gives the start and a ridge descent.

set.descent_text: The usual rappel line goes from a tree at the top, then down and to climber's left to a slung block, then straight down to a fixed nut in a small gully, then to the ground. Alternatively walk down the Hallett Couloir or the couloirs into Chaos Canyon.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. This is the first of the gullies on the Steeplechase buttress above the lake. The route climbs the gully from its base, where it narrows into a steep chimney. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route pages; rappel line sourced from the neighbouring route that shares the top.

set.descent_text: Rappel the line used for No. 1 Gully: from a tree at the top, down and to climber's left past the third belay to a slung block, then straight down to a fixed nut in a small side gully, and one more rappel to the ground. Walking down the Hallett Couloir is the other common choice.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. Look for the snow finger marked 2 on the Steeplechase buttress. The route heads for the steep corner at the back of that gully. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page describes the rappels.

set.descent_text: Walk the ridge in the Bear Lake direction until a gap lets you drop through the terrain park chutes to the trail. In midwinter, rappelling the route is the wiser choice.
set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and hike, ski or snowshoe to Emerald Lake; the going beyond that varies. From the end of the trail at the lake, scramble directly uphill to a little notch above the talus. The route follows a shallow, left-trending gully with a roof about halfway up, on the cliff band on the Emerald Lake side of the ridge that divides Tyndall Gorge from Chaos Canyon. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page: approach and both descents.

set.descent_text: There are no trees, so build a V-thread and rappel. The rappel off the roof is free-hanging for a long way to the ground.
set.approach: In winter, park at the signed East Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir and follow the road to the summer trailhead, then continue south on the East Fork trail; snowshoes are needed and the approach is long. Keep going until the trail begins climbing a long hill. The pillar is briefly visible to the west-northwest, looking like a palm tree. If you reach the sharp left bend at the top of the hill, you have gone too far. Leave the trail, head west to the drainage below the climb, and follow it or the ridge on its right up to the ice. Slopes beside the approach and climb can be hazardous. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page.

set.approach: In winter, park at the signed East Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir and follow the road to the summer trailhead, then continue south on the East Fork trail; snowshoes are needed and the approach is long. Go on to a big meadow; the climb shows up to the southeast beside a conspicuous chute. Quit the trail there, wade the creek, and head southwest to the main ditch that drains the climb. Follow it up to a tight alcove high above the creek. The climb is in an avalanche path, and a slide has run all the way to the creek there. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page; no descent stated.

set.descent_text: Rappel down the flow and then down one of the two approach pitches. The other way off is to cross the rib on the north side (low fifth class on steep snow) and walk down.
set.approach: In winter, park at the signed East Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir and follow the road to the summer trailhead, then continue south on the East Fork trail; snowshoes are needed and the approach is long. Break west off the trail partway along, contour to the creek, cross it, and follow the first drainage that heads up to the west. At a fork take the left (south) branch to a lower amphitheater. From there, a WI2 gully on the left gives access to the upper flow, or a free-standing pillar on the right may form. Without approach ice, a ledge traverse above the lower cliff works but is sketchy with little snow. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page: approach options and descent.

set.descent_text: Anchor choices at the top are the ice itself, trees, or a sturdy willow on the right, and a big tree up and left carries cord. Rappel from one of these.
set.approach: In winter, park at the signed East Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir and follow the road to the summer trailhead, then continue south on the East Fork trail; snowshoes are needed and the approach is long. The flow is tucked into a chimney a couple of hundred yards north of Table for One. Follow the Table for One approach: leave the trail where it passes a fork in the creek, follow the East Fork south to the drainage, and climb the embankment west into the avalanche runout. Then watch to the northwest for a hidden cleft right of an inset gully. Scouting it is hard, so it pairs well with Table for One by traversing north along the cliff foot. The route itself sees little avalanche hazard, but the drainages on the approach do. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page; descent anchors only.

set.approach: In winter, park at the signed East Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir and follow the road to the summer trailhead, then continue south on the East Fork trail; snowshoes are needed and the approach is long. Continue until the climb is due west of an opening in the trees. Quit the trail, wade the creek, and hike due west up the drainage to the foot of the cliff. The long gully above empties onto this route, so the approach and climb are in avalanche terrain, and sun can make the objective hazard severe. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page; no descent stated.

set.descent_text: Build a V-thread and rappel. If a thread is not advisable, a few stunted trees stand near the top and larger trees a little farther along.
set.approach: In winter, park at the signed East Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir and follow the road to the summer trailhead, then continue south on the East Fork trail; snowshoes are needed and the approach is long. Continue to the point where the trail passes a fork in the creek. A large sheet of ice on the cliff comes into view shortly before it. Leave the trail, follow the East Fork south to the drainage below the climb, and go up the embankment to the west into a massive avalanche runout zone below the route. Work up the gully floor or beside it to the cliff. The scale of the avalanche path is obvious on the approach. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page.

set.descent_text: Descents have gone down climber's right, off slung trees on the rock next to the ice. Rappel anchors have been placed for 70 m ropes, but trees are plentiful there, and ice thread anchors are also easy to build.
set.approach: The north face is reached from the Colorado Trail, on the Elk Creek section that runs east from the Animas. Park at the pack-animal trailhead at Molas Park, just south of Molas Lake, descend to the Animas River, cross it, and follow the tracks to the Elk Creek trailhead. Take the Elk Creek trail, crossing avalanche debris piles. At the third pile, go right toward the creek and follow a faint trail between the debris toe and the creek. Stay on the north side through alder and small meadows, then get across Elk Creek on a logjam above the point where the access creek joins from the south. Follow that creek bed, which can have some WI2 ice, then bushwhack and climb scree to the toe of the flow. The route is far from the road and makes a very long day. The approach is exposed to significant avalanche terrain. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route and area pages from the same author; counted as one source. Numbers left out.

set.descent_text: Walk off to the left (west) from the top of the wall.
set.approach: Start at Bear Lake and hike to Emerald Lake. The route is on the south face of Flattop Mountain, between Dream Lake and Emerald Lake; when the ice has formed, go to its foot and climb the slope. The slopes on the approach are avalanche terrain. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page for location and descent; area page for the trailhead.

set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the trail to Emerald Lake, pass around its shore, and angle uphill to the right under Flattop. The route is the obvious open-book corner just right of the Two Dragons line, on the left-hand wall of the Dragon's Tail couloir, a little beyond the big boulder at the foot of the couloir. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page gives the position next to Two Dragons.

set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the trail to Emerald Lake, pass around its shore, and angle uphill to the right under Flattop. The Dragon's Tail is the nearer of two couloirs cutting the south side of Flattop, running up toward the summit area. Snow reaches around 50 degrees, with a few rocky steps that may be iced. A cornice can threaten the upper part early in the season. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area and route pages; no descent stated.

set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the trail to Emerald Lake, pass around its shore, and angle uphill to the right under Flattop. Follow the right side of the lake, taking care with water running under the snow and ice. The couloir is to the left of the Dragon's Tail, and the two are similar types of climb. A snow cornice can form at the top. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Area and route pages; no descent stated.

set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the trail to Emerald Lake, pass around its shore, and angle uphill to the right under Flattop. The couloir lies between the Dragon's Tail and Dragon's Tooth couloirs. Begin in the Dragon's Tooth; beyond its third ledge, a narrow track on the right leads upward into the rock. It joins the top of the Dragon's Tail, where the last section up to the cornice must be climbed. Being narrow and rocky, it warms and thins early, making it an early-season objective. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page; no descent stated.

set.descent_text: The route ends on the summit of Flattop. Descend the Flattop Trail to Bear Lake.
set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the trail to Emerald Lake, pass around its shore, and angle uphill to the right under Flattop. The route climbs the upper headwall on the southeast side of Flattop. From Emerald Lake, work up easy snow and moderate rock to the upper southeast couloir. Climb past a large chockstone, then leave the couloir to the left onto the steep wall below another large chockstone. Expect loose rock, big snow mushrooms and possible avalanche hazard. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page.

set.descent_text: The route joins the South Ridge line higher up. Climbers there walked left along a ledge and made a short rappel to walking terrain. To get back to the base, traverse a long way to skier's right, then return leftward along a ledge system.
set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the trail to Emerald Lake, pass around its shore, and angle uphill to the right under Flattop. The route starts up an obvious splitter on the left-hand wall of the Dragon's Tail couloir, a little beyond the big boulder at the foot of the couloir. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page.

set.approach: From the trailhead, walk the trail southward to a wide meadow where Fall Creek swings away on the left and drops into a gorge. Break off the trail toward the east, reach the creek, and follow the winding canyon down to the lip of the falls. The usual way in is a double-rope rappel, anchored to ice or boulders in the slot at the lip. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page: approach is top-down; exit not stated.

set.descent_text: Descend the less steep, unnamed couloir to the east, which involves some self-belayed downclimbing. The south ridge to Hayden Pass Road is a fallback or rescue exit.
set.approach: Park at the Hayden Creek Campground and walk up the middle fork of Hayden Creek, heading roughly south-southwest. The forest is moderately dense near the stream, so keep to the drainage's eastern side. For the last stretch, turn due southwest and climb a steep slope to the foot of the couloir. All of it is off trail, so carry a GPS track. The line is visible from the highway in Coaldale. The best time is mid-spring after the avalanche conditions have settled. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route page.

set.descent_text: Descend by the peak's standard route.
set.approach: Drive the 4WD road up Yankee Boy Basin as far as conditions allow, then boot up the basin. Gilpin Peak forms the south wall of the basin, facing Sneffels. The couloir sweeps up the north side of the peak. In early season crampons are likely to be needed. Rock releases from the walls as the sun warms the couloir, so start early. Check the avalanche forecast before heading in.

review.notes: Route and area pages.
